title: Physics Basics · Episode 1
chapters: Energy: what it is and where it goes

units.t: Physics Basics. Episode one.
In this episode: Newton's laws of motion, Gravity, Why things float and Energy: what it is and where it goes.
Part one. Newton's laws of motion.
Three simple rules explain why seatbelts save lives, rockets fly, and a heavy trolley is hard to stop.
Newton and inertia.
Newton's great book began with a question.
In 1684, Edmond Halley asked what path a planet follows if the Sun's pull weakens with the square of the distance.
Newton answered at once: an ellipse.
The work grew into the Principia, published in 1687 and paid for by Halley.
It set out three laws still used to design cars, bridges, rollercoasters and spacecraft.
The first law says an object at rest stays at rest, and a moving object keeps moving in a straight line at the same speed, unless an outside force acts on it.
The more mass, the more inertia.
Friction hides this on Earth, so for centuries people believed motion needs a constant push.
In a crash, the car stops but your body keeps moving forward: that is why seatbelts and airbags save lives.
Force and acceleration.
The second law says force equals mass times acceleration: F = ma.
Push an empty shopping trolley and it speeds up easily; push a full one with the same force and it barely moves.
A loaded truck needs far more braking force than a car.
Force is measured in newtons: one newton accelerates one kilogram by one metre per second, every second, roughly the weight of a small apple.
Acceleration happens only when forces are unbalanced.
Friction resists surfaces sliding and is essential for tyres to grip and for you to walk.
Air resistance, or drag, rises rapidly with speed, so driving faster uses more fuel.
A skydiver speeds up until drag balances their weight, reaching about 200 km/h belly-down.
Action and reaction.
When you push on something, it pushes back just as hard in the opposite direction.
When you jump, you push down on the Earth and it pushes you up.
The Earth moves too, but immeasurably little because its mass is so huge.
A rocket pushes exhaust gases backwards at high speed, and they push the rocket forwards.
It needs no air to push against, which is why rockets work in space.
The two forces act on different objects, so they don't cancel out.
The recoil of a gun and the kick of a fire hose are the same law at work.
Momentum and force.
Momentum is mass times velocity, so a slow truck can carry as much as a fast, much lighter car.
In a collision the total momentum stays the same, merely shared differently.
That is why Newton's cradle keeps clicking, and a cue ball can stop dead while the ball it hits rolls on.
Changing momentum takes a force applied over time, so stretching out the time reduces the force.
Crumple zones lengthen a collision, lowering the force on passengers.
Bending your knees when landing from a jump, or a cricketer drawing their hands back to catch a ball, does the same.
Circles and everywhere.
Moving objects travel in straight lines, so anything moving in a circle needs a constant pull towards the centre: centripetal force.
For a car on a corner it is tyre friction; for the Moon, Earth's gravity; for washing in a spinning machine, the drum wall.
The outward 'fling' you feel is not a real force.
It is your inertia trying to carry you straight on.
A footballer's kick accelerates the ball, second law.
A swimmer pushes water back to move forward, third law.
Engineers use the laws for safer car seats and helmets, and NASA still uses them for most spacecraft trajectories.
Newton said he saw further by standing on the shoulders of giants, among them Galileo and Kepler.
The key idea: Objects keep doing what they are doing unless an outside force acts on them.
Part two. Gravity.
It holds you to the ground, keeps the Moon in orbit and shapes galaxies.
It's also the weakest force in nature.
One universal force.
Newton realised the force pulling an apple down is the same one holding the Moon in orbit.
His law of universal gravitation, published in 1687, says every object attracts every other, with a force that increases with their masses and decreases with the square of the distance between them.
Double the distance and gravity drops to a quarter; triple it and it drops to a ninth.
In 1798, Henry Cavendish measured the tiny pull between lead balls in his laboratory, which allowed Earth's density and mass to be calculated.
You are gravitationally attracting the device in your hand right now, just very, very weakly.
Mass, weight and falling.
Aristotle taught that heavy objects fall faster, and for almost 2,000 years few checked.
Around 1600 Galileo showed otherwise, most likely by rolling balls down ramps rather than, as legend says, dropping them from the Leaning Tower of Pisa.
Heavier objects feel a stronger pull but also resist acceleration more, so the effects cancel exactly.
In 1971, Apollo 15 astronaut David Scott dropped a hammer and a falcon feather on the airless Moon, and they landed together.
Your mass, how much matter you contain, is the same everywhere.
Your weight, the force of gravity on that mass, is not.
On the Moon, with about one-sixth of Earth's gravity, a 70 kg person would read about 12 kg on Earth scales; on Mars about 26 kg.
Near Earth's surface, falling objects speed up by about 9.
8 m/s every second.
Orbits and tides.
Newton imagined firing cannonballs from a mountaintop faster and faster, until one curved down exactly as fast as Earth's surface curved away.
It would fall forever without landing: an orbit.
The International Space Station, about 400 km up at roughly 28,000 km/h, circles Earth about every 90 minutes.
Astronauts float not because gravity is absent, since it is about 90% as strong there, but because they and the station fall together.
Geostationary satellites orbit about 36,000 km up, keeping pace with Earth's rotation.
Because gravity weakens with distance, a planet pulls harder on a moon's near side than its far side.
Jupiter's tides melt the interior of Io, the most volcanically active world in the solar system.
In 1992 Jupiter tore Comet Shoemaker-Levy 9 into more than 20 pieces, which hit the planet in 1994.
Weak but winning.
Gravity is by far the weakest of nature's four fundamental forces.
A small fridge magnet holds itself up against the pull of the entire Earth.
Between two protons, electric repulsion is roughly 10^36 times stronger.
Yet gravity rules the cosmos because electric charges, positive and negative, mostly cancel in bulk matter, while gravity only attracts and keeps adding up across unlimited distances.
Newton admitted he couldn't explain how gravity acts across empty space.
In 1915, Einstein's general relativity said massive objects curve space and time, and other objects follow those curves.
So gravity isn't instant: if the Sun vanished, Earth would circle its empty position for about eight minutes.
In 2017, gravitational waves and light from a neutron star collision arrived within two seconds of each other after 130 million years, confirming gravity travels at light speed.
Gravity and your body.
In orbit, without the constant load of weight, astronauts can lose around 1% of bone density in weight-bearing bones each month.
They exercise about two hours a day to limit muscle and bone loss.
Their spines lengthen, making them a few centimetres taller, and fluids shift towards the head, giving a puffy face.
On Earth, gravity squeezes your spinal discs through the day, so you are slightly taller in the morning.
Gravity isn't uniform either: because of Earth's spin and bulging equator, you weigh about 0.
5% less at the equator than at the poles.
The key idea: Every mass attracts every other mass, with a pull that grows with mass and falls with distance squared.
Part three. Why things float.
A steel ship weighing tens of thousands of tonnes floats, yet a small pebble sinks.
The explanation goes back to a Greek genius, and possibly a bath.
The Eureka legend.
The tale goes that King Hiero II of Syracuse suspected his goldsmith had mixed silver into a gold crown.
He asked Archimedes to find out without damaging it.

Stepping into a bath, Archimedes noticed the water rise, realised he could measure the crown's volume by the water it displaced, and ran through the streets shouting ‘Eureka’, meaning ‘I have found it’.
The trouble is that the Roman architect Vitruvius wrote the story down about two centuries after Archimedes died, and some historians doubt it.
Galileo pointed out that the overflow method would be too imprecise for a crown, and suggested Archimedes more likely used a balance and his principle of buoyancy.
Either way, the principle is enormously useful.
Archimedes' principle.
Archimedes wrote a treatise called On Floating Bodies, and its central idea is now known as Archimedes' principle.
When an object sits in water, it pushes some water out of the way.
The surrounding water pushes back, creating an upward force called buoyancy, equal to the weight of the water displaced.
If the object weighs less than the water it can displace, it floats.
If it weighs more, it sinks, though it still feels lighter, which is why you can lift a friend easily in a swimming pool.
The principle works for any fluid, liquid or gas.
It explains why a log bobs on a river and why a helium balloon rises through the heavier air around it.
How a steel ship floats.
Steel is about eight times denser than water, so a solid block of it sinks instantly.
Hammer the same steel into a bowl shape, though, and it can float.
The hull encloses a huge volume of air.
As the ship settles into the water, it pushes aside water and sinks lower until the weight of the water displaced exactly equals the ship's own weight.
At that point it floats.
This is also why a ship sits lower when loaded with cargo, because it must push aside more water to balance the extra weight.
Punch a hole in the hull and let water replace the air, and the balance is lost.
Density and safe loading.
In nineteenth-century Britain, some owners overloaded old, overinsured ships so heavily that they sank with their crews.
Sailors called them coffin ships.
MP Samuel Plimsoll campaigned against the practice, and the Merchant Shipping Act of 1876 made load line markings compulsory.
The Plimsoll line shows how deep a ship may safely sit.
Modern versions have several marks because fresh water is less dense than seawater, and warm water is less dense than cold.
The same idea explains why you float more easily in the sea than in a pool, and why an egg sinks in tap water but floats in very salty water.
The Dead Sea, on the border of Israel, Jordan and the West Bank, is several times saltier than the ocean, so swimmers bob like they're lying on a lilo.
Submarines, fish and balloons.
A submarine floats on the surface until it opens its ballast tanks and lets seawater in.
Heavier now, it sinks.
To rise, it uses compressed air to blow the water back out.
Many bony fish manage the same trick with a swim bladder, a gas-filled sac they inflate or deflate to hover at a chosen depth without constantly swimming.
Buoyancy works in air too.
Heating air makes it expand and become less dense, so a hot air balloon is pushed upward by the cooler, denser air around it.
On 21 November 1783, a balloon built by the Montgolfier brothers carried two men across Paris, in the first free flight with people on board.
Your own body is close to the density of water, which is why a deep breath of air helps you float.
The key idea: The famous bath story is probably more legend than history, but the principle behind it is real.
Part four. Energy: what it is and where it goes.
Energy can't be created or destroyed, only changed from one form to another.
Almost all of it on Earth started in the Sun.
Changed, never lost.
Energy is what makes things happen.
Physicists define it as the capacity to do work, applying a force over a distance.
Kinetic energy is the energy of motion.
Potential energy is stored, like water behind a dam or a stretched rubber band.
There are also chemical, thermal, electrical, light, sound and nuclear forms.
Energy is measured in joules, named after English brewer and physicist James Joule; Australian food labels use kilojoules.
Energy is never created or destroyed.
In the 1840s, Joule showed that a set amount of mechanical work always produces the same amount of heat.
Riding downhill turns potential into kinetic energy; braking turns it into heat in the pads.
When we 'waste' energy, we convert it into forms less useful to us.
Speed squares energy.
Kinetic energy equals half the mass times the speed squared.
Double your speed and your kinetic energy quadruples.
A car at 60 km/h carries four times the energy of the same car at 30 km/h.
The brakes, or in a crash the vehicle and the people inside, must absorb all of it.
That is why braking distances grow so quickly with speed, and why lower limits in busy areas, like 40 km/h school zones, save lives.
Small increases in speed matter more than they feel.
Nothing is 100% efficient.
Old incandescent bulbs turned only about 5% of electricity into light; LEDs use roughly 75–80% less electricity for the same light.
Petrol engines turn roughly 20–30% of fuel energy into motion, while electric motors manage around 90%.
Muscles convert only about a quarter of the energy they use into movement, the rest becoming heat, which is why exercise warms you up.
Heat pumps, including reverse-cycle air conditioners, seem to beat the rules, but they move heat rather than make it, delivering three or more units of heat per unit of electricity.
The underlying principle is the second law of thermodynamics: energy tends to spread out and become less concentrated, which is why perpetual motion machines are impossible.
The Sun's power.
Plants capture sunlight through photosynthesis, feeding almost every food chain.
Coal, oil and gas are the remains of ancient plants and marine organisms, so they are stored ancient sunlight.
Wind comes from the Sun heating Earth unevenly; hydro depends on rain, which depends on the Sun evaporating water.
Sunlight striking Earth in an hour or two carries about as much energy as humanity uses in a year.
The exceptions are nuclear energy, geothermal heat and tidal energy, which comes mainly from the Moon's gravity.
The Sun runs on E = mc², Einstein's 1905 finding that mass is a form of energy.
Fusion converts about four million tonnes of the Sun's mass into energy every second.
One gram of matter, fully converted, would release roughly the energy of 20,000 tonnes of TNT.
Power and your body.
Power is how fast energy is transferred: one watt is one joule per second.
A kettle might draw 2,000 watts or more, a laptop about 50 and a phone charger 5–20.
Electricity bills charge in kilowatt-hours: 1,000 watts for an hour, like running a small heater.
The biggest home users are heating and cooling, hot water, clothes dryers and pool pumps, and standby power adds up.
Energy Rating Label stars and full dishwasher loads help cut bills.
Your body is an energy converter too.
One food calorie is about 4.
2 kilojoules, and Australian labels use 8,700 kilojoules a day as a reference for an average adult, though needs vary.
Even at rest, your brain uses about a fifth of your energy.
The key idea: Energy is the ability to do work, and it changes form without ever being created or destroyed.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What problem do seatbelts solve in a crash?
Answer. Your body keeps moving forward as the car stops.
Question two. If you double the distance between two masses, what happens to the gravitational pull?
Answer. It drops to a quarter.
Question three. Why do some historians doubt the famous ‘Eureka’ story?
Answer. It was recorded about two centuries later.
Question four. What does the law of conservation of energy say?
Answer. Energy changes form, but the total stays the same.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
